title: A Shape Made of Nothing
logline: One mountain that four traditions climb by four different names, and at sunrise it throws a shadow that has a shape, a name and a size, and is made of nothing at all.
human_question: If a thing can have a name, a shape and a size and still be made of nothing, what else that I name every day is like that?

place.what_kind_of_place: A steep, near-conical peak that stands clear of everything around it and is held sacred by four separate religious traditions at once, each with its own name for it and its own account of the mark at the top. It is reached only on foot, by a stepped path that people climb through the night in order to be standing on the summit before the sun comes up. The summit itself is small, crowded and usually above the cloud line.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry the film with the sound off. A thread of electric lights and lamps running all the way up the flank of a black mountain, which from the air reads as a single line of light climbing into the dark. A floor of cloud lying below the summit at first light, with the higher ridges standing out of it like islands. And then, for a few minutes after sunrise, the peak laying a clean, sharp-edged triangle across that cloud, a shape so regular that it looks manufactured, which narrows, slides away and is gone.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Every change in the film is a change of light or of crowd, and none of it is under the crew's control. The line of lamps fills from dusk and empties after dawn. Cloud closes and opens over the valleys. The shadow arrives, shortens and disappears on the sun's schedule. The crowd goes from loud at the bottom to silent and slow near the top, and loud again at sunrise.
place.when_it_looks_best: In season, when the path is lit and busy; out of season the climb is dark and empty and the line of lamps does not exist at all. A clear pre-dawn is needed for the cloud floor and is essential for the shadow, which lasts only a few minutes and only when the eastern horizon is open.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A night-to-dawn mountain film. A line of lights climbing a black ridge, thousands of people going up steps in the cold, cloud filling the valleys below, and one of the rarest sunrise effects in the world arriving and vanishing inside a few minutes. It resolves on its own terms: dusk to dawn, bottom to top, dark to light. Someone who never hears a word of the narration still gets a complete piece with a build, a climb and a payoff.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration rather than an argument. The voice never contradicts anything on screen; it points at what is already visible, four names for one mountain, signboards in several scripts, a hollow in the rock that four traditions read four ways, and finally a triangle on the cloud that anyone can see, that has a shape and a name and a measurable size, and that is not made of anything. The viewer is shown the difference between a name and a thing instead of being told it.

sequence.on_screen: Last light. Drone, high and wide: one peak standing alone above ridges that have already gone dark, the valleys around it turning blue.
sequence.voice: In the villages below, people are setting out tonight to walk to the top of this mountain. They do not all call it the same thing. Four names are in use for the place they are all walking to, and each one comes with its own reason for going.

sequence.on_screen: Full dark. The drone pulls back until the whole flank is in one frame: an unbroken thread of lights climbing it.
sequence.voice: A name is not the thing it points at. The texts are exact about this. A name is what makes something known, and the thing made known is a separate item from the name. One mountain is being made known tonight in four ways at once, and none of them is getting in the way of the others.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, inside the crowd. Painted signboards, printed tickets, a loudspeaker announcement, distances written in more than one script, tea poured at a stall at two in the morning.
sequence.voice: The sound of a word travels through the air and is real. You can hear it arrive and stop. What it means does not travel with it. That lives in whoever is listening. Everyone on these steps is hearing sounds and supplying meanings, and it is working perfectly.

sequence.on_screen: The middle of the night. Steps, breath, fog moving through torchlight, people resting against the handrail, a child asleep on a shoulder.
sequence.voice: None of this is a mistake waiting to be corrected. The texts say the Buddha chose to teach in ordinary words, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that people could follow him. Everyday names were the deliberate method, not a compromise he settled for.

sequence.on_screen: First light at the summit. A small crowded platform; the hollow in the rock at the top; several different observances happening within a few metres of each other.
sequence.voice: Four traditions, one hollow in the rock, four accounts of whose it is. Nobody up here is correcting anybody. Each name carries where a person was taught to come from, and every one of them got its owner to the same place.

sequence.on_screen: Sunrise. The drone turns away from the sun. Across the cloud floor below, the mountain lays down an enormous sharp-edged triangle.
sequence.voice: And there it is. That triangle has a shape. It has a name. You could measure it. It is not made of anything. It is only where the mountain is standing between the sun and the cloud. You are looking straight at the difference between a name and a thing, and it is the most beautiful sight of the morning.

sequence.on_screen: The shadow narrows and slides away as the sun climbs. Within minutes the cloud below is plain white. The crowd starts back down the steps.
sequence.voice: It goes as the sun rises. The mountain is still here, and so are the four names for it. Nothing was revealed by the light and nothing was taken away by it. There were only names, doing their work, all the way up and all the way back down.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests do different jobs. C084 is the machinery: paññatti is both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25], and the sources sort it into meaning-concepts and name-concepts, listing among the meaning-concepts the collective whole, the shape, the being, the direction and the time [C084-P:L27-L41]. The Margaya then separates the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it carries, which is not [C084-M:L21]. C001 supplies the permission: the Pradeepika says the Buddha deliberately taught in everyday names, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that listeners could understand easily [C001-P:L51], which means the four names on this path are not an error to be tidied up. Put on one mountain, the machinery and the permission produce a film in which four name-concepts all work at once, and the mountain itself supplies the demonstration neither concept could stage: a shape-concept, visible to everyone, made of nothing.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That 'which name is correct?' is not the question the sources are asking. C084 alone would make this a film about language. C001 alone would make it a film about truth and error. Together they turn the shadow into the argument: saṇṭhāna-paññatti, the concept of shape, is one of the meaning-concepts the sources list, and here it is at cinema scale, with edges and a size and a name, made of nothing but interrupted light. The pairing also closes off the cheap ending, because the quiet at the summit is not ultimate reality finally showing itself; stone, wind and light are wholes with names on them too.

concept_links.why: The sources define paññatti as both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], and list among meaning-concepts the collective whole, the shape, the being, the direction and the time [C084-P:L27–L41]. A high place is a collective concept of exactly that kind, and each tradition's word for it is a name-concept attached to it. The Margaya's separation of the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it conveys, which is not [C084-M:L21], is what this film can actually observe, because the same air is carrying several names at once. The digest's own limit is load-bearing here: a film must never tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, and the sources' existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories, not a scheme of true and false.

The Pradeepika treats conventional teaching in everyday names as deliberate and legitimate, chosen so that listeners could understand easily [C001-P:L51], which is the ground on which this film can hold several religious vocabularies without ranking them. The film must not go further than that. Where the earlier draft had the names falling silent at dawn to leave what is really there, the digest blocks the move twice: it warns against flattening the analysis into 'nothing is real', and the Pradeepika says the final realities are known by omniscient knowledge rather than by ordinary human knowing [C001-P:L59]. Silence on a summit reveals no ultimate; it only leaves fewer words in the air.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name is a shared agreement rather than the thing it points at, and that plenty of what we name and measure and photograph turns out to be a shape rather than a substance. The proof is on screen and needs no belief: a triangle the size of a valley, made of nothing but a mountain standing in the way of the light.
what_must_be_real: The pilgrims, their names for the mountain and their reasons for climbing. No staged interfaith moment, nobody asked to repeat a name for the camera, and nobody asked to say another community's name for the place. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted or lit for filming. The shadow is filmed on whatever morning it actually appears; it is never simulated, composited or graded into existence. If the naming is genuinely disputed between communities, the film records that it is disputed and does not settle it, on screen or in narration. No date, century or order of attestation for any tradition's claim appears on screen or in the voice. The four names are shown in present use, never in sequence.
position_hint: opening candidate: the simplest possible first step for the whole series, a name and the thing it names coming apart in front of people who are not arguing about it, before anything harder is asked. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Ranking, contrasting or harmonising the four traditions; the film has no interest in which name is older or more correct, and the digest forbids telling anyone their name is wrong.
Drifting into a travel film in which the climb is the subject and the naming is decoration.
Consent for people filmed briefly, at night, in a crowd, in languages the crew may not share.
Implying that dawn, silence or altitude strips the world back to what is really there; the C001 digest rules that reading out, and beat 7 exists to refuse it.
Overreaching into 'nothing is real': the sources keep sound, colour, feeling and mind fully real, and treat conventional wholes as valid in their own domain.
Treating the sources' existent / non-existent pairs as 'true' and 'false' names; they are technical categories.
Filming worship as spectacle, or treating a vow as an interesting custom.
The shadow is a few-minute window on a clear morning and the whole payoff rests on it. There is no second take on the same trip, and a clouded eastern horizon means returning.

Putting the earliest surviving written attestation of any tradition's claim on screen — in narration, a caption or a lower third — would read as ranking the traditions by seniority, which the C084 digest forbids. The dates are documentable and the asymmetry is seductive: no date was found for the earliest written Shaiva identification, and the earliest Tamil literary reference located is itself a Buddhist one. The film carries none of them.
drop_if: The four names turn out not to be in everyday use, only recited for visitors.
Filming cannot happen without disturbing worship or the safety of a crowded path.
The contrast of names can only be obtained by arranging it.

The summit's observances cannot be filmed side by side without arranging them. Custody of the summit is Buddhist and restrictions on pilgrims of other traditions are reported, so beat 5's several-traditions-in-a-few-metres shot may not exist to be filmed. It is checked on a pre-visit and the beat is cut rather than staged.

connections.note: Takes in the strand of names as practical instructions that change what people do, and the guard against telling anyone their name is wrong.
Many names for one thing, then one name everybody uses for something nobody can point at.
A name given to a place by many communities, and a name given to one new person by one family.

selection.reason: Carries the opening episode, and absorbs IDEA-0003's account of names as instructions people act on. Legacy merge recommendations (IDEA-0003) were cleared on 2026-09-25: they came from the retired pre-rewrite review reports, which argued merges while ideas competed for episode slots. Those reports are retired, every idea is now 'keep', and selection happens through Chathura's verdict against a per-group quota. The named ideas still exist as separate candidates with their own locations, so the merge was never executed. This field now records executed merges only.

suggested_location.region: Central highlands, on the Ratnapura / Nuwara Eliya district boundary
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place that supplies the concept and the spectacle in the same frame. Four living traditions name one mountain and one hollow in its summit rock four different ways, in everyday use rather than in theory, which is C084's meaning-concept and name-concept distinction happening in public. And the peak is one of very few in the world that throws a true triangular shadow at sunrise, which hands the film a shape-concept at valley scale: something with edges, a name and a measurable size, made of nothing but interrupted light. No other candidate gives both.

historical_thread.story:
The mark at the summit is a hollow in the rock, and four living traditions hold it to be four different footprints. The documentary history of those four claims can be followed in writing, and the record is one of coexistence rather than succession: for at least eleven hundred years the claims have been written down side by side, by writers who knew perfectly well that the others existed, and none of them has displaced any of the others.

For the Buddhist claim the earliest surviving written record is the Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, whose first chapter gives the Buddha's third visit to the island: after preaching at Kalyani he went to Sumanakuta, and in Geiger's standard English translation 'he rose, the Master, and left the traces of his footsteps plain to sight on Sumanakuta'. The Dipavamsa, the older chronicle of the fourth century CE, recounts the same visits and does not name Sumanakuta or the deity Sumana at all; the addition happens between the two chronicles, which is a fact about surviving manuscripts and not a claim about when anyone began to believe anything. Earlier than either, a group of Brahmi inscriptions was found in the 1960s on the upper terrace, dated on letter forms to somewhere between the third century BC and the first century CE; they are largely illegible and one of them carries the word Bhagava, a Pali epithet of the Buddha. Fa-Hsien, the Chinese monk who was in the island in 411-412 CE, records in Legge's translation that the Buddha 'planted one foot at the north of the royal city, and the other on the top of a mountain, the two being fifteen yojanas apart' - two footprints, a distance between them, and no name for the mountain. Mahayana texts know the same high place as Mount Malaya, where the Lankavatara Sutra is set, and Xuanzang described that mountain in the seventh century without having visited the island. Also in the seventh century the pilgrim Vajrabodhi is recorded as having waited a long time for his chance to climb Lanka-parvata and contemplate the footprint. The Tamil epic Manimekalai, conventionally placed around the sixth century, names the same summit and the same owner: 'In it stands the lofty peak Samanta on whose summit are the feet of Buddha, a ship of righteousness to cross the ocean of birth.' A thirteenth-century Pali poem by the monk Vedeha, the Samantakutavannana, is devoted to the mountain under that name.

The Arabic record is nearly as old and is continuous. Ninth- and tenth-century Arabic geography knows the island as Sarandib and the mountain, in the form al-Rahun or al-Rohoun, as the place where Adam came down; al-Baladhuri in the ninth century calls the island Jazirat al-Yaqut, the island of rubies, and Ibn Shahryar in the tenth gives Saheelan as a second name for it. Hamza al-Jurjani, in the tenth-century Tarikh Jurjan, reports a man finding on the mountain a stone inscribed with the words Uhbita Adam. Ibn al-Jawzi, in the twelfth century, writes that 'the mountains of Sarandib are huge, among them is the mountain on which Adam descended'. Yaqut al-Hamawi in the thirteenth century explains the name, noting that in the language of the Indians dib means island. The fullest account of the climb in any language before the modern period is Ibn Battuta's, in the Tuhfat al-Nuzzar, from his visit in the mid-1340s. He describes the mark as lying on a high black rock on a wide plateau and measuring eleven spans; a minaret named after Alexander and a spring at the foot of the mountain; steps cut into the rock by 'the ancients'; iron pins fixed into the rock with ten chains hung from them, the last of which is called the chain of witness because of the fear that takes hold of the climber there; a cave associated with Khidr holding a well full of fish; and two routes up, which he calls Baba and Mama, for Adam and Eve, the Mama way easier and shorter, the Baba way rough and difficult, with a pilgrim who takes only the easy one counted as not having made the pilgrimage at all. He also records Hindus coming up on pilgrimage in his own century. A fifteenth-century Meccan work, Ibn Ziya's Tarikh Makka, describes an ascent by chains of iron to the imprint.

Latin Christendom enters the record in the same century as Ibn Battuta. Marco Polo's account, in Yule's translation, describes in the island of Seilan 'an exceeding high mountain; it rises right up so steep and precipitous that no one could ascend it, were it not that they have taken and fixed to it several great and massive iron chains', and reports the dispute over the summit as it was put to him: the Saracens say the monument there is the sepulchre of Adam, the Idolaters that it is the sepulchre of Sagamoni Borcan - the Mongolian form of the Buddha's name - and each party claims the teeth, the hair and the dish kept there as belonging to their own. Polo also reports Kublai Khan sending an embassy to the island for those relics. Some fifty years later the Franciscan papal envoy John of Marignolli, in the island around 1348-49 and detained there for four months, measured the mark at two and a half palms and could not settle whether it belonged to Adam, to Saint Thomas the Apostle or to King Josaphat, the Christianised Buddha of the Barlaam legend; he also reports being told that the place was forty miles from Paradise. In the fifteenth century the Chinese Muslim interpreter Ma Huan wrote it down as the impress of the foot of the first ancestor of mankind, A-tan. Zheng He's trilingual stone, dated 15 February 1409, found at Galle in 1911 and now in the Colombo National Museum, records offerings connected with the same mountain in three scripts at once: the Chinese text addresses the Buddha, the Tamil text Tenavarai Nayanar, and the Persian text Allah. Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century European reference works summarised the whole arrangement in one sentence, which is worth quoting because of how flatly it states the coexistence: the hollow in the rock is said 'by the Brahmans to be the footstep of Siva, by the Buddhists of Buddha, by the Mahommedans of Adam, whilst the Portuguese Christians were divided between the conflicting claims of St Thomas and the eunuch of Candace, queen of Ethiopia'.

The mountain's own names accumulate in the same way, and some of them travelled home with the visitors. Sri Pada and Samantakuta or Samanalakanda run through the Pali and Sinhala record; Sumanakuta is the chronicle's form; Mount Malaya, Ratnagiri and Mount Lanka are the Sanskrit and Mahayana forms; Mount Rohana is the form that Arabic borrowed as al-Rahun; Sivanolipathamalai, the mountain of Shiva's light, is the Tamil form; and Adam's Peak is the name that English took from the Muslim and Christian accounts. The island's names moved the same way. Arabic Sarandib, from Sanskrit Simhaladvipa, reached English as Serendip or Serendib, attested by 1708 and taken from the tale of the Three Princes of Serendip published in English in 1722; in a letter to Horace Mann dated 28 January 1754 Horace Walpole coined serendipity from it. Ibn Shahryar's Saheelan is the ancestor of Portuguese Ceilao and of Ceylon.

The written record of access and custody is separate from the record of the claims and equally detailed. The earliest dated evidence for organised pilgrimage is epigraphic: the rock inscriptions of Vijayabahu I (1055-1110), at Ambagamuwa - carved in his thirty-sixth regnal year on two rock faces - and at Gilimale, record that the king went up and worshipped the footprint and that he dedicated the village of Gilimale to provision the pilgrims. Nissanka Malla (1187-1196) went up with his army, and a cave inscription and drawing at Bhagava Lena record it. Under Parakramabahu II (1236-1270) the minister Devapatiraja is credited with improving the road and with fixing iron chains to iron stanchions on the bare rock. Custody itself changed hands more than once: after 1581 Rajasinha I placed the mountain in the charge of Saiva ascetics from South India, who held it for something like a century and a half, and Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747-1780) restored Buddhist custody and appointed Welivita Saranankara to it. Vimaladharmasuriya (1687-1707) is recorded as installing a silver umbrella over the mark. The British arrive as measurers: Lieutenant William Malcolm went up from the Ratnapura side on 26 April 1815 and published his account in the Government Gazette of 10 May, giving the summit platform as 74 feet by 24; John Davy in 1817 measured the mark itself at five feet three and three-quarter inches long and between two feet five and two feet seven wide, edged with a margin of brass and studded with gems, under a roof held to the rock by four iron chains. William Skeen gathered the whole of it into a book printed at Colombo in 1870, Adam's Peak: Legendary, Traditional, and Historic Notices of the Samanala and Sri-Pada.

The shadow entered the written record late, and when it did it arrived as a problem. No pre-modern account found in this research describes it. The earliest description located is a note by Ralph Abercromby in Nature of 8 April 1886, The Sunrise Shadow of Adam's Peak, Ceylon, which opens by taking the sight for granted - 'the phenomena of the shadow of Adam's Peak in the early morning have been remarked by almost every traveller who has visited this island' - and then describes what is hard to credit: just after sunrise the shadow of the peak seems to rise up in front of the spectator, and then suddenly either to disappear or to fall down to the earth. Abercromby returned to it the following year in the Philosophical Magazine under the title The peculiar sunrise-shadows of Adam's Peak in Ceylon, and R. Abbay replied in Nature on 16 June 1887. So the first people to put the shadow in writing did so in order to argue about what a shape made of nothing was doing.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C084's machinery has three parts that this record exercises separately, and the site is right because the written history exercises all three rather than merely resembling one.

First, the distinction between the meaning-concept and the name-concept - between what is made known and what makes it known - is exactly what eleven centuries of writers have been unable to collapse here. Every one of them is pointing at the same depression in the same rock. Ibn Battuta measured it at eleven spans, Marignolli at two and a half palms, Davy in inches; the object held still while the names multiplied. If a name were the thing, four names would have to mean four marks, and the archive would read as four different sites. It does not. It reads as one basis carrying several names, which is the sources' own picture of how a name relates to what it designates, and it is why the film can say the distinction is observable rather than asserted.

Second, the basis here is itself one of the sources' harder cases. The mark is a hollow - stone that is absent - and the sources list among the meaning-concepts the kind that is named by emptiness, the well and the cave. So the thing four traditions have named for a thousand years is not an object placed on the summit but a shape in the missing part of a rock. That is the same category as the payoff shot: the triangle on the cloud has edges, a name and a measurable size and is made of nothing but the mountain standing in the way of the light. The film's beginning and its end are the same kind of item, one cut into stone and one laid across cloud, and the history is what proves the first one has been held, named and argued over for centuries without anybody needing it to be made of anything.

Third, the record shows the sound and the meaning coming apart in the most literal way available. The sources keep the spoken sound ultimately real and the name it conveys not; the name lives in whoever is listening. Here the sounds physically travelled - up the mountain, onto ships, into Arabic, Chinese, Persian, Latin and English - and what arrived at the other end was reshaped every time by the listener, not by the speaker. Rohana became al-Rahun. Simhaladvipa became Sarandib, then Serendip, and then, in a private letter of 1754, a word for finding what you were not looking for. Sakyamuni became Sagamoni Borcan in a Venetian book and King Josaphat in a Franciscan's notes. Saheelan became Ceylon. Nothing was corrupted; the air carried a sound and each hearer supplied a meaning, which is the mechanism the film watches on the steps at two in the morning, running at the scale of centuries and continents.

C001 supplies what stops all this from becoming a film about error. Conventional teaching in everyday names is presented in the Pradeepika as the deliberate method, chosen so that people could understand easily, not a compromise. The archive is the strongest possible demonstration of that method working: the names on this mountain are not decoration on a pilgrimage, they are the instructions that got people up it. Ibn Battuta's two routes are named Baba and Mama and the names tell a climber which path he is on and what his climb counts for. Vijayabahu's inscription names a village and thereby feeds the pilgrims. Zheng He's stone names three recipients in three scripts and thereby makes three offerings. The four names have each been, for somebody, a practical instruction that changed where they walked - which is the strand this idea absorbed from IDEA-0003, and the history is its evidence.

C001 also closes the exit the film must not take. The correction is not the ultimate either. Centuries, palaeographic dates, regnal years, letter forms, 'the earliest surviving attestation' - every one of those is a conventional designation of time and class, and the Pradeepika puts the final realities beyond ordinary knowing. So the historical record cannot be used to settle which name is right, and the film does not try; the record's actual value is that it has never settled it either. The last piece is the shadow's own paper trail. When European science finally wrote the triangle down in the 1880s it immediately fell to arguing about whether it rose, fell or vanished - three centuries of pilgrims had watched it and the first written accounts of it disagree about what it did. A shape made of nothing was given a place in the scientific literature and promptly became contested there too, which is the film's whole point arriving from an unexpected direction.
what_is_certain: The mark at the summit is a hollow, footprint-shaped depression in the rock, and four living traditions hold it to be, respectively, the Buddha's footprint, Shiva's, Adam's and, in the Christian accounts, St Thomas's.

The Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, records in its first chapter that the Buddha left the traces of his footsteps on Sumanakuta; the wording quoted in the story is Geiger's standard English translation as published online at lakdiva.org.lk.

The Dipavamsa, the older chronicle of the fourth century CE, covers the same visits and contains no reference to Sumanakuta or to the deity Sumana. This is a statement about what the two surviving chronicles contain, not about when any tradition arose.

Brahmi inscriptions were found on the upper terrace in the 1960s, dated on letter forms to between the third century BC and the first century CE. They are largely illegible; one carries the word Bhagava, a Pali epithet of the Buddha.

Fa-Hsien was in the island in 411-412 CE and his record, in Legge's translation, states that the Buddha 'planted one foot at the north of the royal city, and the other on the top of a mountain, the two being fifteen yojanas apart'. The text gives two footprints and a distance; it does not name the mountain.
The Tamil epic Manimekalai, conventionally placed around the sixth century CE, names the peak Samanta and attributes the feet on its summit to the Buddha.
A thirteenth-century Pali poem on the mountain, the Samantakutavannana, is attributed to the monk Vedeha.

Ninth- and tenth-century Arabic writing knows the island as Sarandib and a mountain in it, as al-Rahun or al-Rohoun, as the place of Adam's descent. Al-Baladhuri (ninth century) calls the island Jazirat al-Yaqut; Ibn Shahryar (tenth century) gives Saheelan; Hamza al-Jurjani's Tarikh Jurjan (tenth century) reports a stone found on the mountain inscribed Uhbita Adam; Ibn al-Jawzi (twelfth century) writes that among the mountains of Sarandib 'is the mountain on which Adam descended'; Yaqut al-Hamawi (thirteenth century) notes that in the language of the Indians dib means island; Ibn Ziya's Tarikh Makka (fifteenth century) describes an ascent by chains of iron to the imprint.

Ibn Battuta climbed the mountain in the mid-1340s and his account in the Tuhfat al-Nuzzar records: the mark on a high black rock on a wide plateau, eleven spans long; a minaret named after Alexander and a spring at the foot; steps cut by 'the ancients'; iron pins fixed in the rock with ten chains hung from them, the last called the chain of witness; a cave associated with Khidr containing a well full of fish; and two named routes, Baba and Mama, the Mama way easier, with a pilgrim who takes only that one counted as not having made the pilgrimage. He also records Hindus coming on pilgrimage in the fourteenth century.

Marco Polo's account, in Yule's translation, describes in the island of Seilan 'an exceeding high mountain; it rises right up so steep and precipitous that no one could ascend it, were it not that they have taken and fixed to it several great and massive iron chains', and reports the rival claims on the summit monument - the Saracens saying it is the sepulchre of Adam, the Idolaters that it is the sepulchre of Sagamoni Borcan, the Mongolian form of the Buddha's name - together with the disputed teeth, hair and dish, and Kublai Khan's embassy for those relics.

John of Marignolli, a Franciscan papal envoy, was in the island around 1348-49, was detained there some four months, gave the mark as two and a half palms long, and left the question open between Adam, St Thomas the Apostle and King Josaphat, the Christianised Buddha of the Barlaam legend. He also records being told the place was forty miles from Paradise.
Ma Huan, the Chinese Muslim interpreter of the Ming voyages, recorded the mark in the fifteenth century as the impress of the foot of the first ancestor of mankind, A-tan.

The trilingual stone set up by Zheng He is dated 15 February 1409, was found at Galle in 1911, is held in the Colombo National Museum with a replica at Galle, is inscribed in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, and addresses the Buddha in the Chinese text, Tenavarai Nayanar in the Tamil and Allah in the Persian. It is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

The earliest dated evidence for organised pilgrimage is epigraphic and royal: rock inscriptions of Vijayabahu I (1055-1110) at Ambagamuwa, carved in his thirty-sixth regnal year on two rock faces, and at Gilimale, recording his ascent and worship of the footprint and his dedication of Gilimale to provision pilgrims. A cave inscription and drawing at Bhagava Lena record the ascent of Nissanka Malla (1187-1196).

Custody of the mountain is recorded as having changed hands: after 1581 Rajasinha I placed it in the charge of Saiva ascetics from South India, who held it for roughly a century and a half, and Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747-1780) restored Buddhist custody and appointed Welivita Saranankara. These are recorded layers and the film records them as such.

Lieutenant William Malcolm ascended from the Ratnapura side on 26 April 1815 and published the account in the Government Gazette of 10 May 1815, giving the summit platform as 74 feet by 24 feet. John Davy measured the mark in 1817 at five feet three and three-quarter inches long and between two feet five and two feet seven inches wide, edged with a margin of brass and studded with gems, under a roof fastened to the rock by four iron chains.
William Skeen's Adam's Peak: Legendary, Traditional, and Historic Notices of the Samanala and Sri-Pada was printed at Colombo in 1870 and is the nineteenth-century compilation of this material.

The mountain's recorded names include Sri Pada, Sumanakuta, Samantakuta and Samanalakanda, Mount Malaya (the setting of the Lankavatara Sutra), Ratnagiri, Mount Lanka, Mount Rohana, the Arabic al-Rahun or al-Rohoun, the Tamil Sivanolipathamalai, and Adam's Peak.

The island's names travelled through these accounts. Arabic Sarandib derives from Sanskrit Simhaladvipa; English Serendip or Serendib is attested by 1708; the tale of the Three Princes of Serendip appeared in English in 1722; and Horace Walpole coined serendipity from it in a letter to Horace Mann dated 28 January 1754, published only in 1833.

The earliest written description of the sunrise shadow located in this research is Ralph Abercromby's note 'The Sunrise Shadow of Adam's Peak, Ceylon', Nature, 8 April 1886 (doi 10.1038/033532c0), which opens 'the phenomena of the shadow of Adam's Peak in the early morning have been remarked by almost every traveller who has visited this island' and describes the shadow, just after sunrise, seeming to rise up in front of the spectator and then suddenly either to disappear or to fall down to the earth. Abercromby published again on it as 'The peculiar sunrise-shadows of Adam's Peak in Ceylon' in the Philosophical Magazine in 1887 (doi 10.1080/14786448708627975), and R. Abbay replied with 'The Shadow of Adam's Peak' in Nature on 16 June 1887 (doi 10.1038/036152a0).
what_is_disputed: Widely repeated attribution, not verified: that Fa-Hsien climbed the mountain or saw the mark. His record, as translated by Legge, mentions two footprints and does not name the mountain, and the secondary literature itself says it is unclear whether he visited. The film does not put him on the summit.

Widely repeated attribution, not verified: that Marco Polo ascended the peak, and that he described the footprint. The passage translated by Yule describes the mountain, the iron chains and the dispute over a summit sepulchre and its relics; at least one standard reference states explicitly that he does not mention a footprint in the rock, and nothing found here establishes that he climbed it himself. Travel writing routinely pairs 'Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta both climbed it'; only the second is supported.

Widely repeated attribution, not verified: that the ninth-century Arabic account of Adam's footprint on this mountain is by Sulayman the Merchant. The Akhbar al-Sin wa-l-Hind is dated to 237 AH / 851-2 CE, but the standard reference literature gives its author as unknown and describes the attribution to Sulayman as traditional; the text was later expanded by Abu Zayd al-Sirafi. The exact wording of the al-Rahun and Adam passage could not be checked against a scholarly edition, only against secondary quotation. The claim that some ninth-century Arabic writing names the mountain as Adam's is well supported; the named author and the exact wording are not.
Al-Biruni and Abu'l-Fida are commonly listed among the Arabic writers on this mountain. No passage by either was located in this research and neither is used.
The date of Ibn Battuta's ascent. Sources give 1344 and 1347. The story says the mid-1340s.

The earliest written attestation of the Shaiva identification of the mark was not established. The earliest surviving Tamil literary reference found, in the Manimekalai, attributes the feet on the summit to the Buddha, and the Tamil name Sivanolipathamalai is not dated by any source consulted. This is a gap in the desk research and nothing is inferred from it: an absence of an early surviving text is not evidence about the age or the standing of a tradition, and the film does not treat it as such.

The claim, repeated in popular and travel writing, that the Buddhist identification is attested 'from as early as 300 BC', and the further claim that the print is a smaller mark beneath a larger one or was made on a giant sapphire. Neither is supported by anything found here. The Brahmi inscriptions of that period are largely illegible and only the word Bhagava is reported as read; no footprint claim of that date is documented.

Who fixed the chains, and when. The Culavamsa-based secondary accounts credit the minister Devapatiraja with the road and the iron chains on iron stanchions, but place him under Parakramabahu II (1236-1270) in some accounts and Parakramabahu III (1283-1293) in others. Ibn Battuta counts ten chains in the 1340s and Marco Polo's text, earlier, already has 'great and massive iron chains'; Robert Percival, early in the nineteenth century, wrote that the chains looked very old and that who placed them there was impossible to know. The report that one of the chains survives is secondary and unverified. The film treats the chains as attested by several independent writers and their origin as unsettled.

The Christian attributions. Marignolli around 1348-49 records the St Thomas possibility as one of three he could not decide between, which is firm; the further Portuguese-era division between St Thomas and the eunuch of Candace, queen of Ethiopia, reaches this research through nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century European reference works, and no Portuguese primary source for it was checked.

That the shadow is described in ancient chronicles or in early travellers' accounts. This is asserted in modern travel writing and nothing found here supports it. Abercromby's own 1886 sentence about 'almost every traveller' names none of them. What the first written accounts of the shadow actually do is disagree with each other about whether it rises, falls or vanishes.

Above all: the four claims are not adjudicable from any of this and the film does not adjudicate them. What the record establishes is the documentary history of surviving texts - which manuscript says what, and when it was written down. It says nothing about which identification is correct, and the date of a surviving attestation is not the date of a belief. No tradition here is earlier, later, borrowed or derivative on this evidence, and the block must not be read as putting them in an order. Where the naming or the custody is contested between communities, that it is contested is the finding.

what_to_film: The four names in ordinary use, not recited for the camera: on signboards, tickets and painted distance markers, in a loudspeaker announcement, in how a stallholder or a fellow climber tells someone how much further there is to go.
The line of lights up the flank from the air, before moonrise if possible, as one continuous thread rather than as separate lamps.
The stepped path at three separate heights, so the change in the crowd is visible: loud at the bottom, silent near the top.
The hollow in the summit rock, filmed respectfully and without adjudicating whose footprint it is; the four readings belong in the voice, not in the framing.
Several traditions' observances happening side by side in the same few metres at first light.
The shadow, from a position looking away from the sun, wide enough to hold the whole triangle and the cloud floor it falls on. This is the payoff shot and everything else is built around getting it.
The shadow's retreat in real time as the sun climbs, then the plain white cloud after it has gone, which is beat 7's ending.
suggested_location.access: On foot only. Several routes; the two main ones are the shorter and steeper climb from the Hatton side and the longer one from the Ratnapura side. The track is thousands of cement and rough stone steps. In season the trails are lit with electric light, which is what makes the night ascent and the line-of-lights shot possible at all.
suggested_location.best_time: In season, roughly December to May, when the path is lit and busy. A clear pre-dawn is required. The shadow is reported at its best around April.

suggested_location.research_note: Names, elevation, coordinates, season, routes, trail lighting and the shadow phenomenon are from the sources above and are desk research only. Access, permissions, current trail condition and drone rules are unverified. The historical_thread block added on 25 September 2026 is desk research by web search only, none of it checked on the ground or against printed editions. The Mahavamsa wording is Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, chapter I, printed there without verse numbers. The Fa-Hsien wording is Legge's translation as published at Project Gutenberg. Marco Polo is quoted from Yule's translation as reproduced online, not from a print edition. Ibn Battuta, the Arabic writers, the Tamil Manimekalai line, the royal inscriptions, the custody history and the British measurements all come from the secondary sources listed and were cross-read between at least two of them where possible; where they disagree the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved. Every traveller attribution was checked before being written: the ones that could not be sourced - that Fa-Hsien climbed the mountain, that Marco Polo climbed it or described the footprint, that the 851 CE Arabic account is by Sulayman the Merchant, and any passage by al-Biruni or Abu'l-Fida - are held in what_is_disputed as widely repeated attributions and are not used as fact. The three shadow papers were confirmed through their Zenodo records and DOIs; the Nature 1886 text itself is paywalled and its opening sentence is quoted from search indexing of the abstract, not from the full article, and the page numbers were not confirmed. Skeen 1870 was confirmed through its Google Books record and was not read. No date for the earliest written attestation of the Shaiva identification was found, which is recorded as a gap in the research and not treated as a finding about the tradition. The location, the beats, the risks and Chathura's confirmed verdict are unchanged by this research.
